tasks.summary: The Orderly was rebuilt after tutorial study and three judged rounds. It is a rigged 2.6 m figure with five animations (idle, walk, reach, a duck under door frames, frozen), it stands in the game with a real shadow, and all checks pass. tasks.summary: The earning loop is playable. Raise the instrument (hold right mouse or F, or the round button on a phone), turn your back on the Orderly, and the needle climbs and the ticking races as it creeps up behind you; turn round and it freezes. tasks.title: Blinks that grow into a blackout
tasks.why: The owner wants the wait for the car to build: each blink longer than the last, ending in a long dark stretch that drives the crew away from the lift, then a mad dash back with the Orderly after them
todo: Owner's words (2026-11-16): 'The blinks should get longer and longer as the players wait for the elevator, like 15 seconds for a chase to get them away from the elevator and then the players have to make a mad dash back to the elevator with the orderly chasing them.'

First numbers to try (tune by simulation, in src/sim/run.ts): blinks during a wait run 1, 1.5, 2.5, 4, 6 s with shorter gaps each time; the last one before the car is the blackout, 12 to 15 s, timed to end as the car arrives. Today: every 5 to 9 s, always 1 s, wait 25 to 55 s.

Needs with it: (1) emergency floor strips so the crew can find their way in the long dark, while the Orderly stays unseen (heard, not shown: a watched Orderly never moves, so the dark must really hide it); (2) the announcer warns before the blackout so it is never a surprise death; (3) the car waits long enough for a dash back (boarding is 20 s plus holding the door 15 s; check it fits a 40 m run); (4) simulate hundreds of crews: a careful crew that runs, then looks back once the lights return, usually survives; a crew that stands by the lift through the blackout is usually caught; report both rates; (5) fair on every screen in a crew, like the short blinks.

tasks.title: Even voice loudness and thirty more announcer lines
tasks.why: The owner found the voice much quieter after being caught than in the car, and the same lines get tiring
todo: Cause found: recordings are all at the same loudness (-16 LUFS); the game plays the landing speaker at as little as a tenth of the in-car level when you are far from it (VOICE.farMin 0.08 x farLevel 0.75 vs closeLevel 0.6 in src/game/announcer.ts). Fix: floor the far level near 0.55, soften the far low-pass floor to about 1400 Hz, put a compressor on the voice bus, and play taken/wipe/banked lines at the close level wherever the listener is.

Thirty drafted lines wait in .local/voice-new-lines.json (3,086 characters per voice). Merge into assets_src/voice/lines.json with the usual settings, generate ONE take each for Bella and Brian if the script allows (else three takes: about 18,500 characters, total about 31,500 of the 50,000 cap), publish, check the announcer never repeats a line back to back.

tasks.title: A floor where you have to hide
tasks.why: The owner's idea for a later floor: when its entity is angry enough, a voice tells the crew to hide, the lights go out, music starts, and anyone found during the search dies
todo: Owner's words (2026-11-16): 'if the entity is aggro'ed enough, it kicks off a voice that tells players to hide. If they're found before timer goes off, they're killed. Otherwise, the entity follows it's normal rules. (only move when looking etc) The level goes dark, creepy music starts playing, and players have to find a place. You'll have to research how to make a good ai bot that explores rooms so that the challenge is actually challenging. Staying visible and just running away kills you. Once count is finished, moving faster than creep drains health maybe?'

My reading, to confirm with the owner: (1) an anger level rises with noise (sprinting, calls, readings); (2) at the top, the announcer starts a count (about 20 s), lights go out, music starts; (3) when the count ends a search runs for a set time: the entity checks rooms and hiding places; anyone it finds is taken; moving faster than a creep costs health; (4) when the search time is up it goes back to its usual rule. Hiding places come from the props (lockers, under beds, cupboards, behind curtains).

Research before building (one agent, written up in docs): how games make a searcher that feels smart and fair. Start from occupancy / probability maps (the searcher keeps a belief of where players could be and checks the likeliest spots), last-known-position search, a director that nudges it toward players without telling it exactly (Alien: Isolation's two-part design), and hiding-spot checks with tells so a hidden player can hold their breath. Must stay deterministic from the seed and simulate hundreds of rounds: good hiders usually live, runners die, nobody dies to pure luck.

Fits the existing rules: the entity is heard before seen; the instrument could pay most for a reading taken from a hiding place while it searches nearby; a found player goes down rather than out, with something to do within seconds.

gates.title: Builds clean from a fresh clone
Floors are sound
gates.evidence: 800 floors checked by test; one printed map read by eye. Deliberate break used: with stairs removed from the generator, 2 of its 21 tests fail.

gates.title: Rules hold over 500 simulated runs
gates.evidence: Two independent checkers over 500 simulated runs each: 48,882 moments when a player could see the Orderly, and it had moved in none; 33,646 moments when a reading grew, all with the Orderly moving within range of a raised instrument. Deliberate breaks used: a too-narrow idea of 'seen', no grace period, and recording with the instrument lowered. Each failed its test.

gates.title: The Orderly is a real figure
gates.evidence: A re-runnable Blender script builds a rigged figure (7,380 triangles, 39 bones, 5 animations) that loads, animates and casts a shadow in the game; Fable looked at renders and in-game screenshots; five blind critics over three rounds, worst findings fixed each round. Deliberate break used: with the model file hidden, the Orderly browser test fails. Not claimed: that it is frightening. Blind fear scores stayed between 3 and 6 out of 10.

media.caption: The Orderly in the game

gates.title: Heard before seen
gates.evidence: In 104 generated layouts the squeak is audible at least 2.5 seconds before the figure could first be seen, and in the running game the squeak gain is zero while it is watched and rises when it moves. Deliberate break used: with its hearing range cut to 3 metres, the heard-before-seen test fails. The sound itself has not been heard by a person.

gates.title: One player can finish a run
gates.evidence: A browser test plays a whole two-floor run from the car to a reading, a tape, the call, the blinks, the ride down, a second reading and the bank, with a screenshot at each beat and no console errors; it banked 307. Deliberate break used: with players able to see during a blink, two of the three run tests fail.

gates.title: Four players share one world
gates.evidence: Four tabs: same building, each draws the other three, a moved player drawn within 0.5 m, the Orderly frozen at the identical spot on all four screens for 3 s while one watched (0.000 m disagreement), moving on all four within 0.45 s of the watcher turning away. Two browsers connected over the real peer-to-peer path on this PC in 1.6 s and played the same run. Broken on purpose twice: (1) a client that neither holds nor reports the Orderly, (2) a client that holds it but never tells the host; the four-tab test went red both times (and 3 network logic tests for the second), green again after undoing.

Your phone's picture went blank a few seconds into a run: the browser threw the graphics context away. Fixed in the live build three ways. The game now restores the picture when that happens, and shows a notice while it does. Phones use a lighter 8-bit drawing path from the start. Multiplayer is proven in logic. Over 200 simulated sessions with delays up to 250 ms, lost and reordered messages, every frame of every player's screen was checked: 76,782 moments when a player could see the Orderly in two frames running, and it was never drawn in two different places. When delay let the host move it after a player had already seen it, the host put it back where that player saw it (1,532 times, 2 metres at most). No catch ever landed on a player whose own screen showed it. Blinks are dark on every screen for the whole time the host lets it move. Fable's deliberate break: turning screens back on 0.2 seconds early left 21,367 lit frames and failed the blink test.

The run's rules are proven in logic: the car leaves after dropping you, calling it means a loud wait of 25 to 55 seconds, the lights blink while it comes, and you vote to bank or ride by where you stand. Fable changed two things. The blink was 0.35 seconds, which the agent found left a staring crew completely safe (0 of 320 caught); it is now one second, so a crew that only stands and stares is taken in about 1 wait in 5, and has to keep its distance. And the call now wakes the Orderly. Deliberate break: making a tied vote bank instead of ride fails the vote test.

Design tuning by Fable: the Orderly now runs down anyone who runs but creeps up on anyone standing still, and the instrument pays far more in the last metres. Before, the final approach took about a second and a half, too fast to choose when to turn. Now it takes about four seconds, and turning at arm's length earns roughly double what turning at 2.5 metres does. The earning rule's independent checker verified 33,646 moments of recording with no violations.

The Orderly's rule is proven in logic: across 500 simulated runs an independent checker looked at 48,226 moments when a player could see it, and it had not moved in any of them. It moved in 498 runs and caught someone in 150, so the test is not empty. In 104 layouts its squeak could be heard at least 2.5 seconds before it could be seen. Fable broke the rule two ways on purpose (a too-narrow idea of 'seen', and no grace period) and the checker caught both.

Orderly, revision round 2. Fresh blind judges scored it 3/10 and 5/10 for fear: the scores have not improved. Both said the black eye sockets read as sunglasses at game size, and the art director said the grey grinning stick figure echoes three existing characters. The last round goes after exactly that: pale waxy skin, stitched-shut lids, a puffy paper cap, and a smile that runs off the mask onto the cheeks.

Both said the smile reads as an emoji at game size, the legs are sticks, the gown reads as a dress, and it stands like a plank. Fixes are going back to the modeller.
